label: US Sup. Ct. — TransUnion v Ramirez (concrete-injury refined)
body: Holding: Of 8,185 class members whose TransUnion files were marked as potential matches to a Treasury watchlist, only the 1,853 whose reports had actually been disseminated to a third-party business had Article III standing. A label in a database the consumer never sees and that no one ever requests is not a concrete harm.
"No concrete harm, no standing." Risk of future harm without materialisation is generally insufficient for damages standing in federal court.

Why it matters: Sets the federal-court standing bar for privacy-statute claims — pure procedural violations without downstream dissemination/use struggle. Implication for CCPA § 1798.150 class actions: still alive in CA state court (Spokeo doesn't bind state-court standing), but federal removals face a higher bar.
